paragraphs: Transformer training can appear stalled for many steps before its loss suddenly falls. This paper investigates that behavior through low-rank matrix completion: predicting missing entries in a matrix with underlying structure. The researchers express the problem as masked language modeling and show that a BERT model can learn to complete the matrix with low error.

The resulting training curve contains an early plateau followed by a sharp improvement, even though the training procedure and hyperparameters remain unchanged. This creates a concrete setting for examining what changes inside the model when performance improves abruptly. The analysis compares predictions, attention heads, embeddings, and hidden states on either side of the transition.

Before the transition, the model largely copies its masked input; afterward, it accurately predicts missing entries. Attention develops interpretable patterns relevant to matrix completion, while internal representations encode information useful for the task. The authors also examine individual components during training. Together, these observations connect the sudden loss drop to changes in task-relevant behavior within this case study.
neurips-2024-abrupt-learning-in-transfor.tldr: A matrix-completion case study links abrupt improvement in BERT training to emerging task-relevant attention and internal representations.

paragraphs: Statistical Flow Matching treats generation as movement through a space of probability distributions. The paper develops this framework using information geometry and applies it to categorical distributions for discrete generation. Its central idea is that the geometry of distributions should guide how the model moves between them.

The method uses the Fisher information metric to define distances and directions on this space, then follows geodesics, its shortest paths. A smooth, invertible transformation between manifolds addresses numerical stability during training and sampling. This geometric construction also supports optimal transport in training and an interpretation of the flow as movement along the steepest natural-gradient direction.

The authors additionally provide exact likelihood calculation for arbitrary probability measures, rather than relying on variational bounds. They report that SFM learns complex patterns that existing models can miss because of strong prior assumptions. Experiments spanning images, text, and biological data show higher sampling quality and likelihood than the compared discrete diffusion and flow models, supporting the practical value of explicitly modeling distribution geometry.
neurips-2024-categorical-flow-matching-o.tldr: Statistical Flow Matching uses probability-distribution geometry to improve discrete generation and support exact likelihood calculation.

paragraphs: Detecting machine-written text becomes harder when the generating model hides its internal prediction scores. Existing detectors often substitute scores from an accessible surrogate model. However, differences between the surrogate's text distribution and the source model's distribution can undermine detection, particularly when the source is unknown, changes version, or varies across examples.

DALD addresses this mismatch by fine-tuning surrogate models on publicly accessible outputs from models including ChatGPT, GPT-4, and Claude-3. The aim is to make the surrogate's distribution better reflect those of unknown source models without requiring their internal scores. This alignment can be added to existing detection frameworks, including DetectGPT, DNA-GPT, and Fast-DetectGPT.

The authors report state-of-the-art black-box detection performance across evaluated closed-source and open-source models, with a single detector handling text from multiple origins. They also report robustness on revised text and non-English text. These findings support distribution alignment as a way to strengthen existing detection methods while requiring only a modest training investment.
neurips-2024-dald-improving-logits-based.tldr: DALD improves black-box AI-text detection by aligning surrogate models with publicly available outputs from source language models.

paragraphs: Temporal knowledge graphs represent entities and relationships that change over time. Learning compact numerical representations of them requires tracking more than individual relationships: broader patterns among groups of entities can also evolve. DECRL targets these higher-order correlations, which the authors identify as a weakness of existing approaches.

Its deep evolutionary clustering module learns changing groups of related entities. Because those groups can overlap and change across timestamps, the method includes an unsupervised alignment mechanism that matches clusters one-to-one over time. This maintains temporal smoothness. An additional encoder uses a global graph to capture hidden correlations between pairs of clusters, extending the representation beyond relationships within each group.

Experiments on seven real-world datasets report state-of-the-art performance. Relative to the strongest baseline, average improvements are 9.53% in MRR and 12.98%, 10.42%, and 14.68% in Hits@1, Hits@3, and Hits@10. These ranking results support combining evolving groups, continuity across time, and relationships between groups when representing temporal knowledge graphs.
neurips-2024-decrl-a-deep-evolutionary-c.tldr: DECRL improves temporal knowledge-graph representations by tracking evolving entity clusters and hidden relationships between them.

paragraphs: Attention in vision transformers is often understood as grouping similar image features. Yet a feature can also benefit from attending to something different that supplies context. This paper examines both behaviors by studying the interaction between the query and key transformations that determine which tokens attend to one another.

The authors apply singular value decomposition to the query-key interaction matrix. This separates the interaction into paired feature directions, making it possible to inspect which kinds of represented information are connected. Many of the resulting interactions have recognizable semantic meanings, including connections between related objects, between an object's parts, and between foreground and background.

Across many vision transformers, especially those trained for classification, earlier layers attend more to similar tokens while later layers increasingly attend to dissimilar ones. The authors interpret these findings as evidence of perceptual grouping followed by greater contextualization. The analysis offers a way to understand how attention uses both prominent image features and their surroundings, without assuming that all useful attention must connect similar content.
neurips-2024-dissecting-query-key-intera.tldr: Analyzing query-key interactions reveals evidence that many vision transformers shift from grouping similar features toward using dissimilar contextual features.

paragraphs: Some predictive models change the systems they predict, so deploying a model can alter the data it later encounters. Performative prediction accounts for this feedback through a distribution map describing how deployment changes the data distribution. Finding the best model then depends on how accurately that map represents the actual response.

This paper addresses errors in the distribution map with a distributionally robust formulation. It introduces a distributionally robust performative optimum, a solution intended to remain a good approximation to the true optimum when the modeled map differs from reality. The authors establish theoretical guarantees for this robust approximation under map misspecification.

They also show that the robust problem can be expressed as an augmented performative prediction problem, allowing efficient optimization within that reformulation. Experiments examine misspecification at both micro and macro levels and indicate potential advantages over the traditional performative optimum. The contribution therefore combines a robustness-oriented solution concept, guarantees about approximation, and a computational route for obtaining it.
neurips-2024-distributionally-robust-per.tldr: A robust performative-prediction framework accounts for errors in modeling how deployed predictions change future data.

paragraphs: Minimum Bayes Risk decoding selects generated text using utility scores between candidate outputs and reference translations. Its quadratic scoring cost can make it expensive. This paper studies machine translation and asks whether the full table of scores can be reconstructed from a much smaller set of computed entries.

The authors first show empirically that these score matrices have low-rank structure, meaning their entries contain substantial shared structure. They then compute a random subset of utility scores and use Alternating Least Squares to estimate the missing entries. The recovered matrix supports an approximation of the original decoding process while avoiding most direct utility evaluations.

On WMT22 English–German and English–Russian translation in both directions, the method uses one-sixteenth as many utility computations as vanilla MBR while matching translation quality measured by COMET. It also produces significant quality gains over the other approximation methods evaluated. These results show how exploiting the structure of the score table can reduce decoding work while retaining measured translation quality in the reported setting.
neurips-2024-efficient-minimum-bayes-ris.tldr: Low-rank matrix completion approximates MBR decoding with one-sixteenth of the utility evaluations while matching COMET quality in reported translation experiments.

paragraphs: Estimating a camera wearer's body motion is difficult when observations cover only a few body parts and are also intermittent. This paper investigates whether occasional hand poses visible in egocentric video, together with head motion, can meaningfully constrain full-body movement. The authors find that directly applying a diffusion model to these sparse inputs gives suboptimal results.

Their solution divides the problem into two stages. First, a masked autoencoder fills gaps in hand trajectories using relationships across time and between head and hand poses. It also estimates uncertainty in those filled-in observations. Second, a conditional diffusion model uses the now temporally dense head and hand trajectories to generate plausible full-body motion.

Uncertainty from the first stage guides the second, so the completed hand trajectories are accompanied by information about their reliability. Experiments using AMASS and Ego-Exo4D across different head-mounted display setups validate the approach. The findings support handling missing observations over time before reconstructing the unobserved parts of the body.
neurips-2024-estimating-ego-body-pose-fr.tldr: A two-stage method completes intermittent hand trajectories and uses their uncertainty to guide full-body motion generation.

paragraphs: FilterNet approaches time-series forecasting through signal filtering. The paper identifies sensitivity to high-frequency signals, computational cost, and incomplete use of the frequency spectrum as challenges for Transformer forecasters, especially on long sequences. Its alternative learns which frequency components to preserve or attenuate when extracting useful temporal patterns.

The network contains two kinds of learnable filters. A plain shaping filter uses a shared frequency kernel for filtering and temporal modeling. A contextual shaping filter considers how filtered frequencies fit the particular input when learning dependencies. Together, the filters can approximately substitute for linear and attention mappings commonly used in forecasting models.

This design aims to suppress high-frequency noise while still drawing useful information from the full spectrum. Experiments on eight forecasting benchmarks report better effectiveness and efficiency than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The results support learnable frequency filtering as a practical modeling approach, with both the representation of temporal information and the computational demands of forecasting addressed through the same design.
neurips-2024-filternet-harnessing-freque.tldr: FilterNet learns frequency filters that improve forecasting accuracy and efficiency across eight evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: Organizations collaborating through federated learning may have different data, competing business interests, and incentives to benefit without contributing. Data differences can also cause negative transfer, where collaboration harms learning. This paper treats the choice of collaborators as a problem involving both data complementarity and participants' interests.

FedEgoists groups participants into coalitions with shared interests. Its formation strategy enforces two conditions: a participant benefits from federated learning if and only if it benefits the ecosystem, and it does not contribute to competitors or their supporters. These conditions address free riding and indirect support for competitors alongside the learning benefits of collaboration.

The authors prove optimality in a specific sense: no formed coalitions can collaborate together to improve the utility of any of their members. Experiments on established benchmark datasets compare the strategy with nine state-of-the-art methods and support its effectiveness. The contribution is a way to organize collaborative networks that accounts for organizational incentives as well as the usefulness of shared training.
neurips-2024-free-rider-and-conflict-awa.tldr: FedEgoists forms federated-learning coalitions that address free riding and competitive conflicts, with a specific coalition-optimality guarantee.

paragraphs: FVEL connects language models to formal program verification through theorem proving. It translates code into Isabelle and uses an LLM to conduct automated proof search within that setting. This brings Isabelle's organized rules and theorems into the verification process while allowing different language models to be introduced or updated.

The paper also introduces FVELER, a training dataset containing Isabelle-formulated verification processes and code dependencies. It includes 758 theories, 29,304 lemmas, and 201,498 proof steps. The dependencies provide context connecting individual proof steps and results, making the resource broader than a collection of isolated verification answers.

The authors fine-tune models on FVELER and evaluate them in FVEL using Code2Inv and SV-COMP. On SV-COMP, the number of solved problems increases from 69 to 81 for Llama3-8B and from 75 to 84 for Mistral-7B, corresponding to improvements of 17.39% and 12%. Proof errors also become less frequent. These findings support training on structured verification traces to improve LLM-assisted theorem proving for code.
neurips-2024-fvel-interactive-formal-ver.tldr: FVEL combines Isabelle-based verification with language models, and its FVELER training data improves solved-problem counts and reduces proof errors.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning tries to infer rewards that explain demonstrated behavior. Because multiple rewards may explain the same demonstrations, theoretical approaches often estimate the entire feasible reward set. In the online setting, a learner can collect additional information about environmental dynamics, but estimating that set remains difficult when there are many states.

The paper shows that the structure of Linear Markov Decision Processes alone does not make feasible-set estimation efficient in large state spaces. It therefore introduces rewards compatibility, a framework generalizing the feasible-set concept. The resulting CATY-IRL algorithm is sample efficient, with complexity independent of the number of states in Linear MDPs.

For tabular problems, CATY-IRL is minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors, placing its worst-case performance close to the best possible rate. The analysis also establishes the same worst-case rate for reward-free exploration and improves its existing lower bound. A shared framework connects the two problems, making the contribution both a scalable IRL approach and a theoretical link between reward inference and exploration.
neurips-2024-how-does-inverse-rl-scale-t.tldr: CATY-IRL uses rewards compatibility to achieve state-count-independent sample complexity in Linear MDPs.

paragraphs: Personality measurement faces a longstanding question: should psychological traits have one common structure across people, or should each individual have a distinct structure? The idiographic personality Gaussian process, or IPGP, takes an intermediate position. It represents shared trait organization while also allowing person-specific deviations from that organization.

The model builds on Gaussian process coregionalization to describe related responses across grouped survey batteries. It adapts this construction to ordinal responses, where answer categories have an order but are not treated as Gaussian measurements. Stochastic variational inference estimates the latent factors used to characterize these response patterns.

Using synthetic data and a new survey, the authors report better prediction of observed answers and better estimation of within-person response patterns than existing benchmarks. The survey analysis also identifies distinct clusters of personality taxonomies. These results support a measurement approach that preserves population-level structure while accommodating individual variation, with potential relevance to individualized psychological diagnosis rather than an established diagnostic outcome.
neurips-2024-idiographic-personality-gau.tldr: IPGP models shared personality structure alongside individual deviations, improving survey-response prediction and within-person pattern estimation.

paragraphs: Conversational assistants for electronic health records need both relevant instruction-following examples and a way to handle complicated clinical data structures. This paper addresses those two requirements together. It introduces a dataset for adapting general-purpose language models and a framework for processing the heterogeneous information contained in patient records.

MIMIC-Instr contains more than 400,000 open-ended instruction-following examples derived from MIMIC-IV. The examples cover varied topics and are intended to support diverse clinical uses. The accompanying framework, Llemr, enables language models to process and interpret complex EHR structures, connecting instruction tuning with the particular demands of record-based questions.

Llemr shows competitive performance when answering a broad range of patient-related questions using EHR data. On clinical prediction benchmarks, the fine-tuned framework performs comparably to state-of-the-art baselines that use curated features. Together, these findings support the combination of instruction data and structured-record processing as a route toward more capable EHR language models across both question answering and predictive modeling.
neurips-2024-instruction-tuning-large-la.tldr: MIMIC-Instr and Llemr combine large-scale instruction data with EHR processing to support patient questions and competitive clinical prediction.

paragraphs: Jailbreak attacks try to make language models produce objectionable content despite their safeguards. Comparing attacks is difficult when studies use different definitions of success, count costs differently, or withhold the prompts and code needed to reproduce results. JailbreakBench provides shared evaluation infrastructure to address these problems.

The benchmark combines an evolving collection of adversarial prompts with a dataset of 100 behaviors drawn from both new material and prior work. It specifies the threat model, system prompts, chat templates, and scoring functions used in evaluation. These details establish a common procedure for testing attacks rather than leaving important experimental choices implicit.

A leaderboard tracks attacks and defenses across language models, while the open prompt repository makes evaluated artifacts available for inspection and reuse. The contribution is a reproducible basis for comparison, rather than a claim that a particular defense solves jailbreaking. The authors also acknowledge ethical considerations surrounding release and judge the benchmark's expected community impact to be positive.
neurips-2024-jailbreakbench-an-open-robu.tldr: JailbreakBench standardizes jailbreak evaluation through open prompts, a 100-behavior dataset, shared scoring procedures, and a leaderboard.

paragraphs: LoRA reduces fine-tuning costs by training a small low-rank addition to a pretrained model. However, cheaper training iterations do not automatically produce cheaper training overall: the paper reports that standard LoRA often converges more slowly than full fine-tuning and can achieve worse test performance. It investigates initialization as a source of improvement.

LoRA-GA initializes the low-rank parameters so that the gradient of their matrix product approximates the full-fine-tuning gradient at the first step. The architecture and subsequent training algorithm remain unchanged. This makes the starting point of adaptation the central intervention, directing the restricted update toward the initial change that full fine-tuning would make.

Experiments report convergence comparable to full fine-tuning, with comparable or better performance and observed convergence speed improvements of up to two to four times over vanilla LoRA. On a GLUE subset with T5-Base, the reported average improvement over LoRA is 5.69%. Additional gains on Llama 2-7B support the usefulness of gradient-aware initialization across the evaluated model settings.
neurips-2024-lora-ga-low-rank-adaptation.tldr: LoRA-GA accelerates low-rank fine-tuning by initializing its updates to approximate the initial gradient of full fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Image diffusion models contain internal activations that can also serve as features for recognition tasks such as semantic segmentation. Choosing a compact, effective subset is difficult because many activations are available. This paper argues that previous comparisons overlooked useful candidates, including attention queries and keys and signals inside embedded vision-transformer modules.

Expanding the candidate pool makes exhaustive quantitative evaluation impractical. The authors instead analyze activation properties to identify clearly inferior candidates through simple qualitative assessment before further selection. They report three properties shared across diffusion models and use them to guide feature-selection solutions for several widely used architectures.

Experiments across multiple discriminative tasks show better performance than the compared state-of-the-art approaches. The central contribution is therefore both broader coverage of potential features and a way to make selection manageable. By using properties that extend beyond an individual model, the approach aims to avoid repeating an exhaustive search whenever a diffusion architecture exposes a new collection of internal signals.
neurips-2024-not-all-diffusion-model-act.tldr: A broader analysis of diffusion activations enables practical feature selection and improves performance on evaluated recognition tasks.

paragraphs: An agent adapting across different embodiments must learn what transfers between them while retaining information about their distinct characteristics. Previous cross-embodiment approaches often learn knowledge tied to particular tasks. This paper introduces cross-embodiment unsupervised reinforcement learning, where agents interact online without task rewards to acquire task-independent, embodiment-aware knowledge.

The authors formalize this setting as a Controlled Embodiment Markov Decision Process and analyze pretraining objectives within it. Their resulting algorithm, PEAC, supplies an intrinsic reward designed specifically for learning across embodiments. Although the environment provides no task reward during this phase, the intrinsic signal gives the agent an objective for exploration and learning.

PEAC can also be combined with existing unsupervised reinforcement-learning methods to support exploration and skill discovery across embodiments. Experiments in DMC, Robosuite, and real-world legged locomotion report significant improvements in adaptation and cross-embodiment generalization. These findings support pretraining that explicitly accounts for embodiment differences before specializing an agent to a downstream task.
neurips-2024-peac-unsupervised-pre-train.tldr: PEAC uses embodiment-aware intrinsic rewards during task-reward-free pretraining to improve adaptation across different embodiments.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients collaborate without sending their private data to a central server, but many systems require every client to use the same model architecture. pFedClub addresses the more flexible setting where client models differ and each client needs a personalized result. Its approach operates on interchangeable network blocks or layers.

The server first divides heterogeneous models into blocks and groups them by function. A Controllable Model Searching and Reproduction algorithm constructs multiple candidate models for each client. A matching step then selects the best personalized candidate to serve as a teacher that guides that client's training.

Experiments cover three datasets under both IID and non-IID data settings, testing collaboration with more uniform and more heterogeneous data distributions. The authors report state-of-the-art performance over the compared baselines. Their model analysis also finds that the approach controls personalized model size and significantly reduces computational costs. The findings connect architectural flexibility with practical personalization through the selection and reuse of functional model components.
neurips-2024-pfedclub-controllable-heter.tldr: pFedClub recombines functional blocks from heterogeneous client models to create controllable personalized teachers for federated learning.

paragraphs: New reinforcement-learning tasks can require substantial interaction, especially when success depends on completing several subtasks over a long horizon. MGPO addresses this challenge by pretraining a Transformer policy to follow sequences of goals. Adaptation then centers on choosing a useful goal sequence, which acts as the policy's prompt.

Pretraining combines behavior cloning with hindsight multi-goal relabeling. This uses task-agnostic data to teach behaviors associated with varied goal sequences. During online adaptation, the method evaluates prompts through the returns of actual trajectories and optimizes their selection using a multi-armed bandit framework.

This structure links prior behavioral learning to feedback from a new task: the policy already models diverse long-horizon behaviors, while online interaction helps identify which goal sequence works well. Experiments across several environments report substantial advantages in sample efficiency, adaptation performance, robustness, and interpretability over existing methods. The results support goal-sequence optimization as a useful route for adapting pretrained policies with fewer interactions in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2024-pre-trained-multi-goal-tran.tldr: MGPO adapts pretrained Transformer policies to new tasks by optimizing goal-sequence prompts using online returns.

paragraphs: Giving a language model more chances to answer does not necessarily teach it to improve on previous attempts. RISE targets that capability directly through fine-tuning. It trains models to revise unsuccessful responses to difficult problems, optionally using additional feedback from the environment as they work through successive turns.

The method recasts a single-prompt task as a multi-turn Markov decision process whose initial state is the prompt. Its data collection and training strategies draw on online imitation learning and offline reinforcement learning. This formulation makes detecting and correcting earlier mistakes part of the behavior the model is trained to perform.

Experiments with Llama2, Llama3, and Mistral show improved reasoning performance as models receive more turns. RISE outperforms several single-turn strategies when inference-time computation is held equal, indicating benefits beyond simply spending more compute. The authors also report that stronger models often gain more and that the training does not disrupt one-turn abilities, supporting learned revision as a complementary capability.
neurips-2024-recursive-introspection-tea.tldr: RISE fine-tunes language models to revise failed attempts, improving multi-turn reasoning under matched inference-compute comparisons.

paragraphs: Separating a scene from its reflection in a single image becomes especially difficult when the two are densely mixed and reflection intensity varies widely across the image. The paper attributes weaknesses in earlier dual-stream methods to limited spatial context and insufficient modeling of relationships between the features exchanged by the streams.

The proposed Dual-Stream Interactive Transformer addresses relationships both within and between the two image layers. Dual-stream self-attention captures correlations inside each layer, while layer-aware cross-attention captures correlations across them. Attention also expands the spatial context available to the model, helping address the limited receptive field identified in earlier designs.

The method further combines pretrained Transformer embeddings with convolutional features from both streams through cross-architecture interactions. This supplies richer semantic information to help resolve an inherently ambiguous separation problem. Extensive experiments show advantages over the compared state-of-the-art alternatives. The contribution is a coordinated interaction design that uses layer relationships, wider context, and pretrained semantic features to improve reflection separation.
neurips-2024-single-image-reflection-sep.tldr: DSIT improves single-image reflection separation by combining within-layer and cross-layer attention with pretrained semantic features.

paragraphs: Predicting a person's next point of interest from past visits is complicated by the uneven popularity of places. Some locations receive many visits, while many others receive few, making the less-visited destinations difficult to predict. LoTNext addresses this long-tail problem as part of next-location prediction.

The framework intervenes in both the user-location graph and the training objective. A graph-adjustment module reduces the impact of long-tailed nodes in the interaction graph. A loss-adjustment module changes prediction scores and sample weights, providing another way to account for the uneven distribution during learning. An auxiliary prediction task is also used to improve generalization and accuracy.

Experiments on two real-world trajectory datasets show significant gains over the state-of-the-art methods evaluated. The approach matters because it treats visitation imbalance as a problem affecting both the representation of user-place interactions and how prediction errors shape training. The reported results support this combined treatment for mobility prediction, a task relevant to navigation, recommendations, and urban planning.
neurips-2024-taming-the-long-tail-in-hum.tldr: LoTNext improves next-place prediction by addressing visitation imbalance in both interaction graphs and training losses.

paragraphs: Chain-of-thought prompting can improve language-model reasoning, but understanding its capabilities requires more than observing whether a prompt helps. This paper develops a reasoning boundary framework to quantify the upper bound of chain-of-thought capabilities and provide guidance for improving performance. It addresses measurement and optimization within one formulation.

The authors define a reasoning boundary and a combination law for boundaries, aiming to make quantitative assessment practical across real-world reasoning tasks. They then introduce three categories of boundaries and use combination laws to guide improvements. The two optimization perspectives are raising reasoning boundaries and improving the paths used to reach an answer.

Experiments across 27 models and five tasks support the proposed framework, and the authors use it to explain the effectiveness of ten chain-of-thought strategies. The resulting contribution is a vocabulary and quantitative structure for relating observed reasoning capabilities to optimization choices. Its experimental support concerns the evaluated models and tasks, while its broader aim is to make reasoning improvements more systematic.
neurips-2024-unlocking-the-capabilities-.tldr: A reasoning-boundary framework quantifies chain-of-thought capabilities and guides improvements to capability limits and reasoning paths.

paragraphs: USCILab3D is an outdoor dataset built from a year of robot traversals around the USC campus. A teleoperated robot carried five cameras and a 32-beam LiDAR scanner with full surrounding coverage. Collection across varied paths, weather, and lighting provides repeated observations under changing conditions within the campus's roughly 92.7 hectares.

The dataset includes 10 million images and 1.4 million point clouds, totaling approximately six terabytes. Foundation models were used to annotate the raw observations. Processed outputs include multi-view imagery, 3D reconstructions, images and point clouds labeled with 267 semantic categories, and textual descriptions of images and objects. Pose and trajectory information support additional analyses.

Its stated tradeoff is geographical breadth for denser coverage: it covers less area than a whole-city dataset but emphasizes intricate intersections and rich multi-view observations. The authors describe this density as enabling more precise 3D labeling and a wider range of 3D vision tasks. The contribution is a long-term, multimodal resource for research across vision, robotics, and machine learning.
neurips-2024-uscilab3d-a-large-scale-lon.tldr: USCILab3D provides a year of densely sampled campus imagery and LiDAR with semantic annotations, reconstructions, text, and trajectories.
